title: Wireshark SocketCAN upgrades
description:
This patchset simplifies the CAN packet type detection as it focusses
on the rules to distiguish the different CAN CC/FD/XL frames from the
Linux kernel API.

Additionally some more content is shown in the dissector and the
CAN CiA 611-1 definitions have been cleaned up and extended by CiA.

When you use the full struct can_frame (aka can_frame_t) or struct canfd_frame (aka canfd_frame_t) with 16 resp. 72 bytes everything is fine.

But if you start to "optimize" the CAN CC/FD frames by the data length, you would need different flags and content to put these information together:
- a CANFD_FDF flag
- a RTR flag
- ESI/BRS flags
- a value containing DLC values from 9..15 for CAN CC frames

All this content is described in my PR for the pcap HTML documentation:
https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/tcpdump-htdocs/pull/37

But with this approach we are merging the two protocols of CAN CC and CAN FD into one - instead of giving them two different and independent layouts.

Wireshark already relies on the independent CC/FD layouts by testing the frame length to be 16 or 72.

And e.g. your example https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/wiretap/busmaster.c also uses can_frame_t and canfd_frame_t when writing the CAN frames to their wsbuffer. So everything is fine. The use of 16/72 byte structures seems to be common use. And that busmaster.c is setting the (optional) CANFD_FDF flags is also ok.

Maybe I got something wrong. But is turns out that relying only on the frame size (16/72) and having different structures is already common sense. Maybe the documentation for CAN CC/FD should also split up there.

Just an additional comment to https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/wiretap/blf.c
In fact BLF uses the "optimized" length approach. But it has problems with CAN CC RTR and DLC length's.

I would suggest to clean up and fix blf.c to support reading and writing the correct 16/72 frame sizes.

And to be compatible to former recorded pcap log files, we might check the CANFD_FDF flag when the size is NOT 16/72 (btw. a CAN FD frame with 8 byte of data also has a frame length of 16 with the "optimized" length - so we would always need to test for CANFD_FDF here). But in the end we should really try to get away from the CANFD_FDF usage in pcap/Wireshark.

I can see the problem now.

> I would suggest to clean up and fix blf.c to support reading and writing the correct 16/72 frame sizes.

In what sense are those sizes "correct"?  Are the padding bytes transmitted on the wire, so that the Vector Informatik products that write BLF files are discarding those bytes, or is the SocketCAN code putting padding bytes into the packets it provides?

At least as I read 8.4.2.4 "DLC Field" of ISO 11898-1, the data field is variable-length, and 10.4.2.5 "Data field" says that "the MAC data field shall be equivalent to the LLC data field".  Is padding inserted at the physical layer for some or all physical layers?

Note als that BLF files contain, in the CAN packet metadata, more information than is available in SocketCAN metadata, so perhaps BLF CAN packets should have their own WTAP_ENCAP_ type and provide the additional metadata in their own metadata headers, with a separate dissector for those packets, and common code to hand off the data field, with any necessary accompanying metadata, to payload dissectors.

> In what sense are those sizes "correct"? Are the padding bytes transmitted on the wire, so that the Vector Informatik products that write BLF files are discarding those bytes, or is the SocketCAN code putting padding bytes into the packets it provides?

The Linux CAN socket API has two C structs for the CAN CC and CAN FD frames:

- struct can_frame (sizeof(struct can_frame) = 16 = CAN_MTU)
- struct canfd_frame (sizeof(struct canfd_frame) = 72 = CANFD_MTU)

See https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v6.8.1/source/include/uapi/linux/can.h

These two structs can be read from the socket or be written to the socket. Depending on the size (16/72) the Linux kernel and the application knows whether it deals with a CAN CC or CAN FD frame.

The CAN driver get's these structs and puts the content into the registers of the CAN controller which then sends the CAN frames on the wire. When there are only 4 data bytes defined in the data length the real CAN frame which is sent on the bus also contains only 4 data bytes.

> At least as I read 8.4.2.4 "DLC Field" of ISO 11898-1, the data field is variable-length, and 10.4.2.5 "Data field" says that "the MAC data field shall be equivalent to the LLC data field". Is padding inserted at the physical layer for some or all physical layers?

No, there is no padding on the physical layer.

> Note als that BLF files contain, in the CAN packet metadata, more information than is available in SocketCAN metadata, so perhaps BLF CAN packets should have their own WTAP_ENCAP_ type and provide the additional metadata in their own metadata headers, with a separate dissector for those packets, and common code to hand off the data field, with any necessary accompanying metadata, to payload dissectors.

I wonder if it really helps to have tons of metadata about CAN. The description of a CAN frame consists of a timestamp, the CAN bus interface and the CAN frame (with its flags, identifier and data).
IIRC the Vector tools also provide e.g. the frame length in bits and some more statistics and a more detailed error detection and CAN controller status. I've never needed such information but I have no idea if someone else needs it.

Hello @guyharris 

I updated the pull request for libpcap (force push) here:

https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/libpcap/pull/1296

and created a new pull request for Wireshark here:

https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/14946

These two changes re-enable the optimized data length support that seems to be used by the BLF converter together with DLT_CAN_SOCKETCAN.

And it also reduces the libpcap sanitizing effort to the minimum as it only ensures the correct required flag usage.

 /*

  */
-#define CANXL_SDU_TYPE_CONTENT_BASED_ADDRESSING	                 0x01

-#define CANXL_SDU_TYPE_CLASSICAL_CAN_MAPPED_TUNNELING            0x06
-#define CANXL_SDU_TYPE_CAN_FD_MAPPED_TUNNELING                   0x07
+#define CANXL_SDU_TYPE_CONTENT_BASED_ADDRESSING 0x01
+#define CANXL_SDU_TYPE_CAN_CC_CAN_FD            0x03
+#define CANXL_SDU_TYPE_IEEE_802_3               0x04

+#define CANXL_SDU_TYPE_CAN_CC                   0x06

+#define CANXL_SDU_TYPE_CIA_611_2                0x08

commits_data.title: socketcan: display len8dlc content for Classical CAN
commits_data.message:
socketcan: display len8dlc content for Classical CAN

While the Classical CAN frame can transport only 8 byte of data the
4 bit data length code (DLC) has the ability to have a value range
from 0 to 15. To be able to send and receive DLC values from 9 to 15
the struct can_frame contains an additional len8dlc element which
can have values from 9 to 15 when the data length value is 8.

Signed-off-by: Oliver Hartkopp <socketcan@hartkopp.net>

commits_data.title: socketcan: display CANFD_FDF and CANXL_XLF flag content
commits_data.message:
socketcan: display CANFD_FDF and CANXL_XLF flag content

Display the officially defined bits for CAN XL and CAN FD.
While CANXL_XLF is a mandatory set bit value for CAN XL frames
the CANFD_FDF bit might be set based on the used Linux kernel
version. So both bits present valuable content for the user.

Signed-off-by: Oliver Hartkopp <socketcan@hartkopp.net>

commits_data.title: socketcan: simplify CAN packet type detection
commits_data.message:
socketcan: simplify CAN packet type detection

The different CAN frame types are defined by Linux SLL_P types in the
sll_protocol field and the length of the frame.

LINUX_SLL_P_CANXL:
The frame length for CAN XL can be 12 + 1 to 12 + 2048 (13 .. 2060) byte.
Additionally the CANXL_XLF flag has to be set.

LINUX_SLL_P_CAN and LINUX_SLL_P_CANFD:
The frame length for CAN CC is 16 byte and for CAN FD it is 72 byte.
Additionally the CANXL_XLF flag is cleared in CAN CC/FD frames.

Simplify the CAN packet type detection by checking exactly the above
rules without checking the CANFD_FDF flag which is not guarantied
over all Linux kernel versions.

Signed-off-by: Oliver Hartkopp <socketcan@hartkopp.net>
